## What is an AI employee, and is AI staff the same thing?

An AI employee is AI software you assign outcomes to, not just questions. It plans a multi-step job, uses tools such as a browser, email, and connected apps to finish it, and keeps the context for the next job. AI staff, AI workers, and AI teammates are the same idea under different labels: Sintra and Marblism sell named "AI employees," Relevance AI uses "AI Workforce," and Lindy's documentation and site use both "AI employee" and "AI teammate."

Underneath the labels, three questions separate these products more than any name does:

1. **Fixed role or any task?** A roster gives you a social media manager or a receptionist with a narrow job. A general-purpose AI employee takes whatever you assign and decides which tools to use.
2. **Does it have its own computer?** An agent with a browser, files, and a terminal can work in tools that have no integration. A chat-first product is limited to what its integrations expose.
3. **How is the work metered?** Seats, credits, hours of work, and plan limits behave very differently when a busy month runs over.

Construct answers all three the way a small team needs: any task, its own workspace, and plan pricing with no seats. Our explainer on [what an AI employee is](/blog/what-is-an-ai-employee/) covers the definition in more depth.

## Methodology

We build Construct, so it leads this list; here is why it fits small teams: it takes any recurring job, keeps the files, schedule, and memory for that job in one shared workspace, and starts at $9 a month without per-seat pricing. We ranked the other nine by how well they fit a small team's recurring work across apps, then by entry price and what happens at the limit.

This is an editorial comparison of documented capabilities and published prices, checked on September 29, 2026 against each vendor's own pricing pages, documentation, and announcements. Construct's plan details were updated on October 1, 2026. It is not a hands-on benchmark of output quality.

We included products that appear in search results for "AI employees" and "AI staff for business" and that a small business can start without a sales call, with two deliberate additions: Artisan, the best-known AI sales employee, and OpenClaw, because running your own agent is a real alternative to paying for any of these. Prices are in US dollars at monthly billing unless we say otherwise. Where a capability is not documented, we say so rather than treating silence as proof it is missing. Where a vendor's pages disagree, we report both figures.

We left out Motion, whose AI Employees product page now redirects to its homepage and whose AI Employees help articles no longer load, and Soleur, whose hosted product was still marked "Coming Soon." Enterprise-only platforms are outside the scope of this list.

## The 10 best AI employee platforms, ranked

### 1. Construct

**Best for:** founders and small teams that want recurring work, its files, and its schedule in one place.

Construct runs your agents in a persistent cloud workspace with files, a live browser, a sandbox terminal, and its own email inbox. Give it an outcome, such as "every Monday, check these three competitors' pricing pages and save a dated comparison," and it works out the browser, app, and file steps. Everything it produces lands in workspace files as the run goes, so your team can open the result next week without scrolling back through a chat.

- **Apps:** a live integration catalog with services such as Gmail, Notion, Linear, and HubSpot, plus custom MCP tools when a catalog entry does not exist.
- **Recurring work:** save a job that works as a workflow and put it on the Calendar. Scheduled runs happen on Construct's servers, with your laptop closed.
- **Memory:** inspect what the agent has learned, correct a fact, or forget it, so one fix carries into every later job.
- **Internal apps:** when several people review the same output, Construct builds a private workspace app, such as a review queue or lead tracker.
- **Team use:** team workspaces with Owner, Admin, and Member roles and no member limit. Usage draws on the owner's plan, so there is no per-seat bill.
- **Channels:** assign work from the web desktop, @mention it in Slack, message it on Telegram or Discord, or email its own address.
- **Models:** bundled models on every plan, and on Pro your own keys for OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, or xAI.

    Your browser does not support this video. The description below explains the
    demo.

    Silent product demo: Construct builds and runs a reusable workflow with
    agent steps, connected apps, and notifications, which can be versioned,
    scheduled, and run again by anyone on the team.

**Price:** Lite is $9 a month for 2 agents, 50 steps per task, 3 scheduled tasks, and an agent email address. Starter is $59 with 6x Lite's usage, 5 agents, 150 steps per task, and 10 scheduled tasks. Pro is $299 with 32x Lite's usage, 15 agents, up to 1,000 steps per task, 50 scheduled tasks, and your own model keys, and it comes with a 7-day trial. Annual billing lowers each plan. [Construct pricing](/pricing/) has the current limits.

**Set up deliberately:** workflows run in a straight line and do not pause for approval yet, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself once you have checked them.

### 2. CellCog

**Best for:** hiring one AI employee into a defined role that works in scheduled shifts.

CellCog lets you hire a general-purpose AI employee into a role. Each one gets an email inbox, a task board, persistent memory, and a cloud computer, and with your approval it can work in your own logged-in Chrome. It works scheduled shifts, files a report after each one, and lists more than 1,500 tool integrations.

**Price:** credit plans start at $8 a month for 800 credits and rise to $500 a month for 50,000. CellCog's own plan labels call the $160 tier a part-time employee working "a few shifts a month" and the $500 tier a full-time employee working weekday shifts. New accounts start with 200 free credits.

**Watch for:** CellCog's pricing FAQ says all payments are final and non-refundable, and plan credits expire. Its pages do not name the underlying model providers or offer bring-your-own keys.

### 3. Manus

**Best for:** research, analysis, and build tasks you hand over one at a time.

Each Manus task runs in a sandbox virtual machine with a browser, persistent files, and the ability to install software. Manus 2.0, launched September 28, 2026, adds a desktop app, an always-on Cloud Computer, and control of your own machine. Automations run on a schedule or on app events, and you can reach it by email, Slack, or Telegram.

**Price:** Pro starts at $20 a month for 4,000 credits plus 300 refresh credits a day, with 20 scheduled tasks. Team is $20 per seat a month with a shared credit pool. The always-on Cloud Computer is an add-on from $30 a month.

**Watch for:** credit use varies with task complexity, monthly credits do not roll over, and you cannot start a task with zero credits. If the subscription lapses, the Cloud Computer shuts down and its files are deleted. Manus returned to [independent operation](https://manus.im/blog/manus-resumes-independent-operations) on September 1, 2026 after Meta's acquisition was unwound.

### 4. Lindy

**Best for:** teams whose work already happens in Slack.

Lindy Teammate is an AI coworker in Slack: each person gets a private assistant in direct messages and the team shares one in channels. It connects to an integration catalog and MCP servers, can drive a browser, runs Routines on a schedule or on events, keeps memory as versioned files, and reaches you over iMessage and SMS. Write actions wait for your approval.

**Price:** billed per user. Plus is $29.99 a month with 3,000 credits, Pro is $99.99 with 15,000, and Max is $199.99 with 35,000. Lindy's docs put a credit at about one cent and pool credits across the workspace.

**Watch for:** anyone who uses Lindy takes a paid seat, including someone who only mentions it in Slack. When the credit pool runs out, work pauses until you top up. Lindy's pricing page lists computer use as included everywhere, while its docs show it from Pro upward.

### 5. Grok Bot

**Best for:** people who already pay for Cursor or an eligible SuperGrok plan.

Grok Bot gives you named Bots that share one persistent cloud computer with a browser, files, and a terminal. They sign into your tools, run routines on a schedule or on events, can learn a routine by watching you, and ask for approval before actions you have not allowed. You work with them through desktop and mobile apps.

**Price:** there is no standalone plan. Access is included with Cursor Pro at $20 a month, Pro+, Ultra, and Teams, or with an eligible SuperGrok or X Premium+ subscription linked to a Cursor account. Usage resets weekly and is described in relative tiers rather than published numbers.

**Watch for:** it is labeled beta. Because Bots share one computer, its documentation says not to treat separate Bots as a security boundary. Each Bot can hold up to 50 routines. Our [Grok Bot comparison](/blog/grokbot-alternative/) goes deeper on how it differs from Construct.

### 6. Sintra

**Best for:** a solo owner who wants marketing, social, and admin help without designing anything.

Sintra sells 12 named AI employees, including Soshie for social media, Penn for copywriting, Seomi for SEO, Cassie for customer support, and Vizzy as an executive assistant. They share a knowledge base called Brain AI, run recurring tasks, and can use a built-in browser. Sintra's own FAQ says every AI worker runs as a chatbot.

**Price:** one plan, Sintra X, includes all 12. It lists at $97 a month, and when we checked it was on sale at $48.50 for a one-month term, with lower monthly equivalents for 3- and 12-month terms billed upfront. Every term includes 250 credits a month.

**Watch for:** Sintra's help center says the AI employees stop working when credits run out, and credit top-ups are non-refundable. Its own pages disagree with each other on standard prices and on how many integrations it has.

### 7. Marblism

**Best for:** a local business that wants calls answered along with inbox and social help.

Marblism's roster has seven AI employees: Eva (executive assistant), Sonny (social media), Stan (lead generation), Penny (SEO blog posts), Rachel (phone receptionist), Linda (legal documents), and Walter (websites). Rachel answers calls, transfers them, and texts you summaries, with numbers available in five countries.

**Price:** the base plan is $44 a month, or $24 a month billed yearly, for all seven employees and 50 "hours of work." Each task costs a fixed amount of that time: sorting an email is 20 seconds, a phone call 10 minutes, and a blog post an hour. Larger plans go up to 10,000 hours.

**Watch for:** Marblism documents that Eva drafts emails but does not send them. It has no public API and says one is not on its roadmap. When hours run out, scheduled tasks are cancelled and Rachel's line pauses.

### 8. Relevance AI

**Best for:** sales and support teams that want to design their own agents and multi-agent teams.

You build agents and multi-agent Workforces in Relevance AI's low-code builder, or ask its Invent agent to draft one, and connect them to its app catalog. Agents can run on a schedule, call Python tools, make outbound phone calls on higher tiers, and use the model you pick, including through your own keys.

**Price:** the public pricing page shows only an Enterprise plan with a "Talk to sales" button. Relevance AI's documentation still lists Pro at $29 a month ($19 billed annually) with 2,500 actions and $20 of model and tool credits, and Team at $349 a month. Confirm with the vendor before you plan around either.

**Watch for:** there is no dedicated agent computer, and browser automation runs through a third-party tool, Airtop, on your own account. Failed tool runs still count as actions. SSO and audit logs are Enterprise features.

### 9. OpenClaw

**Best for:** technical owners who want full control and are comfortable running a server.

OpenClaw is a free, MIT-licensed personal AI agent stewarded by a non-profit foundation. You run its gateway on your own computer or a small server, connect any model with your own keys, and chat with it from WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, and other channels. It can browse, run shell commands, edit files, keep memory, and run cron jobs.

**Price:** the software costs nothing, and there is no paid tier. You pay for hosting, where its docs suggest a small always-on server, and for model usage.

**Watch for:** installing, updating, securing, and keeping it online is your job. Its security documentation assumes one trusted operator per gateway, says third-party skills should be treated as untrusted code, and warns that container setups expose the gateway by default and need authentication. Our comparison of [building your own AI agent](/blog/construct-vs-diy/) covers that tradeoff.

### 10. Artisan

**Best for:** outbound sales teams that want an AI BDR to prospect and write outreach.

Artisan's Ava finds and enriches leads from a database of more than 250 million contacts, writes and sends email sequences from your own mailboxes, handles replies, and books meetings. It is a sales employee only.

**Price:** Artisan's default pricing tab is sales-led. A separate Startups track lists an Intern plan from $280 a month ($250 billed annually) for about 500 leads contacted, plus a free plan without campaigns. Mailboxes and phone numbers are billed separately.

**Watch for:** Artisan says Ava cannot legally make calls, so its dialer is for your human reps. Each primary mailbox is capped at 100 sends a day, and new enrollments pause when credits run out.

## How to choose an AI employee platform

Choose by the first job you will hand over, where requests arrive, and what each platform does in a busy month. In order:

1. **Start from the job, not the category.** Write down the one job you would hand over first. If it crosses apps or changes from week to week, you need a general-purpose AI employee such as Construct; a roster covers only its named roles.
2. **Check where the work arrives.** Construct takes requests from the web, Slack, Telegram, Discord, and its own email inbox, so it meets your team where it already talks.
3. **Price the busy month.** Assume twice the work you expect and check what each vendor does at the limit.
4. **Test recurring work, not a demo.** Run the same job three weeks in a row and check whether later runs start from the earlier files and corrections. Construct keeps both in the workspace.
5. **Know what you can inspect and correct.** Ask where memory lives, whether you can edit it, and what record a run leaves behind. [AI agent memory you can control](/blog/ai-agent-memory/) explains why that matters.
6. **Decide who operates it.** Self-hosting saves the subscription and spends your time instead.

Our guide to [choosing an AI agent platform for your team](/blog/how-to-choose-an-ai-agent-platform-for-your-team/) turns these questions into a longer checklist. If you only need a one-off answer or draft, see our [comparison with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini](/blog/construct-vs-chatgpt/); for fixed rules-based routing, [AI agent vs Zapier](/blog/ai-agent-vs-zapier/); and for weighing an AI employee against a human assistant, our [cost comparison with virtual assistants](/blog/ai-agent-vs-virtual-assistant/).

## Already using another AI employee? Add Construct in 15 minutes

You do not have to cancel what you have. Start with the one recurring job your current tool handles least reliably, or the one your teammates need to see.

1. **Start on Lite for $9, or take the 7-day Pro trial** to test your own model keys and longer runs.
2. **Copy the instructions** you gave your current agent into a Construct chat, and move the source files into the workspace.
3. **Connect the apps** the job needs from the integration catalog.
4. **Run it once and check the result** in Files.
5. **Put it on the Calendar** so it runs every week with your laptop closed.

There is no import from other platforms: agents, credentials, and learned memories do not transfer. Write your rules into the first instruction and Construct saves them as memory you can read.

## When might another platform still fit?

- Your first job is answering the phone, which Marblism's Rachel covers.
- Outbound sales at volume from a built-in lead database is the whole job, which is Artisan's focus.
- You want to run the agent on your own server with no subscription, which OpenClaw allows.

For recurring work that crosses apps and has to leave files, schedules, and corrected memory behind, Construct is the better fit.

Choose Construct. It starts at $9 with no per-seat fee, takes any job rather than one role, saves every finished file in a workspace your team shares, runs schedules with your laptop closed, and lets you correct what it remembers. If you already use one of the others for a narrow role, keep it there and give Construct the recurring work around it.

Give Construct its first job

Pick the weekly report, competitor price check, or lead list that keeps slipping into your evening. Give Construct the inputs, describe what a finished file contains, run it once, and put it on the Calendar. Start on [Lite at $9](/pricing/), or try Pro free for seven days, and judge it on the third run, not the first conversation.

**What is the best AI employee platform for a small business?**

Construct, for most founders and small teams. It starts at $9 a month with no per-seat fee, takes any job rather than one fixed role, saves finished work in a workspace your team shares, runs Calendar schedules with your laptop closed, and lets you inspect and correct what it remembers. We build Construct, which is why it leads our list, and we checked the other nine against their own pages on September 29, 2026.

**How much does an AI employee cost?**

Entry prices checked on September 29, 2026 run from $0 for self-hosted OpenClaw, plus hosting and model costs, and $8 to $9 a month for CellCog and Construct, to $29.99 per user for Lindy and $280 a month for Artisan's sales agent. Most platforms meter work with credits, hours, or seats, so price a busy month. Construct Lite is $9, Starter is $59 for up to 5 agents across the whole workspace, and Pro is $299 with a 7-day trial.

**Is AI staff the same as an AI employee?**

Mostly, yes. Vendors use AI employee, AI staff, AI worker, and AI teammate for software agents given a job rather than a single prompt. The differences that matter are whether the agent has a fixed role or takes any task, whether it has its own computer, and how its work is metered.

**What happens when an AI employee runs out of credits?**

It depends on the vendor. Lindy pauses work until you top up, Sintra's AI employees stop working, Marblism cancels scheduled tasks and pauses its phone receptionist, Manus cannot start new tasks, and Artisan pauses new enrollments. Construct publishes its plan limits up front; you can move up a plan, and on Pro continue on your own model keys.

**Can I use Construct alongside another AI employee?**

Yes. Keep a role-based tool for its narrow job and give Construct the recurring work around it. There is no import, so copy your current agent's instructions into Construct, move the source files into the workspace, connect the apps, run the job once, and put it on the Calendar.

**Can an AI employee answer phone calls?**

Some can. Marblism's Rachel answers calls, transfers them, and texts you summaries, and Relevance AI offers outbound phone calls on its higher tiers. Artisan says its AI sales rep cannot legally make calls. Construct has no built-in phone agent, so a phone-first job is one of the few cases where another platform still fits.
## Nobody merges an email

URL: https://construct.computer/blog/agent-verification-gap/
Type: article
Author: Ankush
Published: 2026-09-22
Tags: ai-agent, reliability, product, ai-employee

It is 5:40 on a Friday and the agent has just written nine client updates in four minutes, sitting there quietly pleased with itself. Eight of them are fine. One of them has told a client something that is not true, and because nothing in the pipeline can tell you which one, you read all nine. Forty minutes later you send eight, rewrite one, and work out that the time you saved on the writing came straight back out of your evening. The agent did not save you thirty six minutes. It moved them, out of writing, which you are decent at, and into checking, which nobody is good at and nobody enjoys.

Every tool you actually work in has an undo. Git has revert, your editor has a keystroke, staging has the comfort of breaking somewhere that does not count, and Gmail gives you thirty seconds. Nobody merges an email: there is no diff to skim, no test suite to run it past, no staging inbox to try it in, and no way back once it is sitting in somebody's inbox, so the entire cost of being wrong lands on one person reading carefully. That gap, and not the model, is why your agent is trusted with code and kept well away from the account manager's inbox. It is also why most agent pilots quietly stall.

Meet Construct

## The bottleneck moved and the tooling stayed put

Software is the one place where a lot of people pointed agents at real work and then measured what happened. The measurements are not subtle.

Faros AI compared two years of telemetry from 22,000 developers across 4,000 teams, looking at each organization at its lowest and highest AI adoption. Output went up. So did everything that output costs you.

    The two shortest bars are the benefit. Everything longer is what the benefit
    cost. From Faros AI's 2026 report, The Acceleration Whiplash.

A third more tasks per developer, and five times the median review time ([Faros AI, 2026](https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash)). That is not a tooling problem or a model problem. That is a system that got very good at producing work and no better at absorbing it.

LinearB looked at the same squeeze from the other end, across 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams in 42 countries, and found the detail that gives the game away.

    AI-assisted work waits more than five times longer for someone to start
    reviewing it, then takes slightly less time to review than human work once
    they do. From LinearB's 2026 Engineering Benchmarks Report.

Read those two bars again. Once a reviewer actually starts, the AI-assisted change is *faster* to get through than the human one: 194 minutes against 252 ([LinearB, 2026](https://linearb.io/blog/8-million-prs-engineering-productivity)). The delay is not the reading. The delay is everything before the reading: the queue, the size of the thing, the sinking feeling, the decision to start.

The expensive part of verification was never the mechanical act of checking. It is the willingness to be the person who signs off.

## Why software absorbed the flood anyway

Engineering took that hit and mostly kept moving, and it is worth being precise about why, because the reason is not talent or process maturity. It is that code is the most verifiable artifact a company produces, and it has been getting more verifiable for forty years.

    Every finished piece of work raises the same five questions. Software spent
    four decades building cheap answers to all of them. Nobody built the other
    column.

A diff is a strange and wonderful thing. It turns "read this 400 line change" into "read these 40 lines that differ", which is a reduction of an order of magnitude in what a human has to hold in their head. Tests turn "is it correct" into a boolean somebody else already thought about. Staging turns "will this break" into "it did not break over there". A pull request turns approval into a record with a name on it. Revert turns a mistake into an inconvenience.

None of that exists for the work most of a company actually does.

There is no diff for an email. There is no staging environment for a CRM. No test suite asserts that the invoice you generated has the right billing period on it, and no button unsends the reply to a customer.

So when an agent produces that kind of work, the verification cost lands entirely on a human with no instruments, and it lands per unit of output. Double the output, double the checking. That is the whole story of why the demo felt like magic and the rollout felt like a second job.

## The check has to be cheaper than the doing

Here is the arithmetic nobody puts in the pitch deck.

Let **D** be what it costs you to do the job yourself. Let **C** be what it costs to check the agent's version. Let **p** be the chance it is wrong in a way you would care about, and **R** the cost when a wrong one gets through: the apology, the refund, the client who stops replying.

Delegating pays when:

```text
C + p x R

| Work the agent finished     | What you check it against                | Cost to check      | Cost if a bad one gets through |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| A code change               | A diff, a test run, a staging deploy     | Minutes, tool-assisted | A revert                   |
| Nine client emails          | The nine source threads, from memory     | Nearly the cost of writing them | A relationship    |
| 200 CRM records updated     | Nothing. You spot check twelve and hope  | Unbounded, so people skip it | A quarter of bad data |

Notice what happens in the bottom row. When C is unbounded, people do not pay it. They either check nothing and silently accept **p x R**, or they stop using the agent for that work. Both look like "the agent did not work out". Neither is about the agent.

This is the same shape as [the half-life problem](/blog/agent-task-half-life/): a per-step property that looks fine up close and decides everything at scale. There, it was reliability compounding over a long run. Here, it is verification cost compounding over volume. Both get fixed by changing the structure of the run, not the intelligence inside it.

Try Construct

## Nobody is measuring this, including you

The obvious objection is that if verification were really eating the gains, people would notice.

They do not notice. That is the best-documented part of this whole argument.

METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 real tasks in repositories they already maintained. Before starting, the developers forecast that AI tools would make them 24% faster. Afterwards, having done the work, they believed they had been 20% faster. Measured, they took 19% longer.

    A 39 point gap between what it felt like and what happened, from people with
    hundreds of hours of prompting experience. From METR's July 2025 randomized
    controlled trial.

These were not novices fumbling with a new toy. Nearly all of them had dozens to hundreds of hours of prior experience prompting models ([METR, July 2025](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)). The generation felt fast, because it was. The review, the correction, the second pass to understand what had been written for them: that time was real and it did not register.

Now scale that error up to a company. MIT's Project NANDA, working from more than 300 publicly disclosed deployments, 52 interviews, and 153 survey responses, put the share of enterprise GenAI pilots with no measurable impact on the P&L at roughly 95% ([MIT NANDA, 2025](https://mlq.ai/media/quarterly_decks/v0.1_State_of_AI_in_Business_2025_Report.pdf)). People have argued about that methodology ever since. Nobody has argued that the number is small. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic projects to be canceled by the end of 2027, citing costs and unclear value ([Gartner, June 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027)). DORA, surveying nearly 5,000 professionals, landed on the phrase that ties it together: AI is an amplifier ([DORA, 2025](https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/)). It makes a system with good feedback loops better and a system without them worse, faster.

Most business processes have no feedback loops at all. They have a person who would notice eventually.

Agents rarely fail an evaluation. They fail an audit nobody ran.

## Five things that make agent work checkable

If verification cost is the constraint, then the interesting engineering is not in the agent loop. It is in everything the agent leaves behind. Five properties do most of the work, and none of them require a better model.

### Artifacts, not transcripts

A chat transcript is the worst possible verification surface: linear, long, and it buries the output inside the reasoning. A file is the best one. You can open it, skim it, diff it against last month's, hand it to someone else, and know at a glance whether the thing exists yet.

The rule is that finished work should be an object you can point at, not a passage you have to read to the end of.

### A draft state before anything irreversible

This is the missing diff, and it is mostly a product decision rather than a research problem. Generate the email, do not send it. Compute the 200 CRM updates, write them as a table first. Produce the invoice as a file before it goes to the customer.

A draft turns an irreversible action into a reviewable artifact, which moves it out of the unbounded row of that table and into the cheap one. The work is identical. The verification cost is not.

### Provenance on anything the agent believes

Half of checking is not "is this right", it is "where did this come from". An agent that says the client's renewal is in March is unverifiable. An agent that says the renewal is in March, learned from the contract PDF you uploaded on 14 August, can be checked in four seconds.

That is why [agent memory needs provenance and correction](/blog/ai-agent-memory/) rather than a vector blob. Memory you cannot audit is a claim you have to re-derive, which is verification cost with extra steps.

### A bounded record of what it touched

Not the full trace. Nobody reads the full trace. What you need is the ledger: what did it touch, when, and why. It is the difference between a stack trace and a receipt.

The test is whether someone can answer "what did it actually do yesterday" in under a minute without reading a single model output.

### Reversibility where it exists, a human where it does not

Some actions can be undone, and those should be cheap to approve. Some cannot, and pretending otherwise is how teams get burned. Sending mail, moving money, posting publicly, deleting records: for those the honest answer is that a person confirms, and the product's job is to make that confirmation a two second glance rather than an investigation.

## How Construct is built around the check

We build [an AI employee](/blog/ai-employee/) with a real computer, so this is the problem we live in. A few things follow directly from the argument above.

Work lands in a workspace filesystem as files, not as messages in a thread. That is the artifacts rule, and it is also why a run that dies partway through leaves usable output behind rather than a transcript to excavate.

Every action goes into Activity: what it affected, when it ran, and why. That is the receipt, not the stack trace, and it exists so the answer to "what did it do overnight" is a scroll rather than a project. Alongside it you get the files it produced, the tool records, and a read-only terminal transcript when you want to go deeper.

Memory is inspectable and correctable, with provenance and temporal context, so a claim can be traced to where it came from and fixed in place instead of argued with. Repeatable work becomes a saved workflow you can read before you schedule it. Current workflows are linear, which is a real limitation and also the reason a workflow is something you can hold in your head.

And the part we have not finished: Construct does not currently insert a mandatory approval gate before every external side effect. Drafts, interruption mid-run, and Activity give you a lot, but if a step sends a customer email or moves money, that step still needs supervision before you let it run unattended. We would rather say that plainly than let someone discover it on a Sunday.

## The next 10x is not in the model

Every agent product is currently competing on the part that got commoditized. Producing plausible work is close to free and getting freer.

The scarce thing is a human's willingness to sign their name under it, and that is bought with diffs, drafts, receipts, provenance, and undo. Software has had those for forty years and, funnily enough, software is the one place agents are actually working.

The rest of the company is waiting for someone to build them the other column.

Put Construct to work

### Frequently asked questions

**Why does an AI agent save less time than it looks like it should?**

Because producing the work got cheap and checking it did not. Delegation only pays when the cost of checking the output, plus the chance it is wrong times what a wrong one costs you, comes in under the cost of doing the job yourself. Reading nine agent-written client emails closely enough to be responsible for them can approach the time it would have taken to write them, at which point the agent is a net loss even when every draft is correct.

**What is the verification bottleneck in agent work?**

The point where output volume outruns a human's capacity to approve it. Faros AI's 2026 telemetry across 22,000 developers found tasks completed per developer up 33.7% while median review time rose 441.5%. LinearB's 2026 benchmarks, drawn from 8.1 million pull requests, found AI-assisted changes wait more than five times longer for a reviewer to start, then review slightly faster than human work once someone does. The expensive part is the decision to sign off, not the reading.

**Why do agents work better for code than for other business work?**

Code carries verification tools that other work does not have. A diff shows exactly what changed, tests and CI let a machine check it, staging lets you try it without consequences, a pull request records who approved, and revert undoes it. An email, a CRM update, or an invoice has none of those, so the entire cost of checking lands on one person with no instruments, per unit of output.

**How do you make AI agent output easier to check?**

Five properties do most of the work, and none need a better model: finished work as artifacts you can open rather than transcripts you must read; a draft state before anything irreversible, so an email or a bulk update becomes reviewable before it happens; provenance on anything the agent believes, so a claim can be traced to its source; a bounded record of what it touched, when, and why, which is a receipt rather than a stack trace; and reversibility where it exists, with a human confirming where it does not.

**Does Construct ask for approval before an agent sends an email?**

Not as a mandatory gate on every external side effect. Construct gives you work as files in a persistent workspace, Activity records of what each action affected, when it ran, and why, inspectable and correctable memory, and the ability to interrupt a running turn. Steps with irreversible effects such as a customer email or a payment still need supervision before you let them run unattended.
## Grok Bot Alternative: Construct vs Grok Bot

Construct gives you an AI employee with its own workspace, files, schedules, and email address from $9 a month, with no other subscription needed first. Grok Bot comes bundled with a Cursor Pro ($20) or SuperGrok ($30) subscription, and its settings documentation says Cursor manages model selection, with no model picker.

For founders and small teams, Construct is the better choice. It costs less to start, lets you bring your own model keys, keeps memory you can read and correct, and builds small private apps so your team can review repeated work in one place. Already have Grok Bot through Cursor or SuperGrok? Keep it, and give Construct the recurring jobs your team needs to see.

## Why choose Construct over Grok Bot?

- **$9 a month, on its own.** Construct Lite includes 2 agents, 3 scheduled tasks, and an agent email address. Grok Bot access arrives with a $20 Cursor Pro or $30 SuperGrok subscription.
- **Your own model keys.** Construct Pro runs on your keys for OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, or xAI. Grok Bot's [settings documentation](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/settings-and-notifications) says Cursor manages model selection and there is no model picker.
- **Memory you can read and fix.** Open what Construct has learned, correct a fact, or forget it, so a stale preference stops costing you rework every week.
- **Private apps for repeated work.** Construct builds review queues and trackers inside your workspace, and a failed edit leaves the last working build in place.
- **Work that outlives the run.** Reports and files land in the workspace as they are produced, so a run that stops at step 30 keeps steps 1 to 29.
- **One team workspace, many channels.** Invite teammates as Owners, Admins, or Members with no member limit, and reach the agent from the web, Slack, Telegram, Discord, or its own email inbox.

## What is Grok Bot?

Grok Bot is the agent product from the company behind Grok. You assign work to bots that use a cloud computer, sign into tools, and coordinate across tasks. The [Grok Bot introduction](https://x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot) describes parallel bots, shared context, routines learned by demonstration, and access through eligible Grok and Cursor subscriptions. ## Where does Construct give you more control?

Both products give an agent a computer. Construct also lets you decide which tools it reaches, how your team reviews its output, which model it runs on, and what it remembers.

### Connect the tools your business actually uses

Construct finds supported applications through its live integration catalog, including Gmail, Notion, Linear, GitHub, HubSpot, and Airtable. You can also add custom MCP tools, so the agent reaches a system through an interface your team provides.

An agency that keeps client approvals in a small internal service, for example, can expose the current approval status as a custom tool. Construct then reads it alongside the report files, without waiting for a new catalog entry.

## A practical example: the weekly client report

Imagine a small agency preparing a Friday account update. This is an illustrative workflow, not a customer case study or a measured comparison.

Once it is right, save the steps as a workflow and put it on the Calendar, where it uses one of Lite's 3 scheduled tasks and runs whether or not anyone is online. Dated reports give next week's job a reference, and a small workspace app can track who has checked each one. The [workflow guide](/blog/ai-workflow-automation/) walks through each step.

There is no import: bots, credentials, and learned memories do not transfer. Write your rules into the first instruction and Construct saves them as memory you can read. One thing to set up deliberately: Construct's workflows run in a straight line and do not pause for approval yet, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself once you have checked them.
